chapter: Chicago friends: Tesch, Stacy and Wettling
title: Being an idol while still alive
summary: Freeman and Dance discuss how history now brings back musicians in their seventies and eighties, and whether Stacy wants the rat race.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Looking back: no regrets, what it all meant

blocks.x: Well, anyway, I think we have given enough time to that, Bud, and actually -- in actuality we really have brought ourselves to the point of where you're --

Yes, excuse me, dear, I want to get this added thought in and perhaps it's a redundant thing to say and maybe it's an original thing to say, but as regards one becoming an idol after he dies, I think the amazing thing that there are men still playing and playing well in their seventies and eighties and perhaps nineties which history never realized was going to happen.

Because history seemed only to tend to idolize the man and make of him a great figure after he died and now what is history going to do about the guys who are still alive and what is history going to do and what is it doing. It is bringing the men back to a musical life the man could never had before he became an idol and Jess Stacy now is a living legend. It's a marvelous thing.
But does he know this and is he willing to give the rest of his life to the dedication of playing
around the world. I just wonder because --
No, I don't think he is --
He would rather have the peaceful life.

I think he is probably torn and possibly, you know, possibly, he would like to be flashes of something, you know, but I don't think -- I really don't think he is prepared to sit down and maintain a standard which he would need to maintain, his own standards, to work rather steadily professionally.
But I am sure that he would be very tempted if he actually realized and knew that the things were at the stage that they are, I think he would be tempted.
